# P8: Ship

```yaml
id:       P8
size:     L
requires: [P2, P5, P6, P7]
blocks:   [final submission]
parallel: [P9 except T8.4]
```

**Goal:** A disclosed demo history, a deployment that survives judging, and a submission that explains itself.

Every task here runs through the loop in `AGENTS.md`: implement, review, remediate, re-review, land. Read that file in full first. Each task block below is written to be handed to an agent on its own.

---

## Where things stand, 14 September

- **Live.** The web app at `orma.nryn.dev` carries P6 (deployed 10:50Z). The API front door is `orma-api.nryn.dev`. The functions are `tick`, `materialise`, `calle-webhook`, `telegram`, `mcp`, `auth-telegram` and `analysis`.
- **Schedulers.** `tick-runs` runs every minute, `materialise-runs` at 00:10 UTC, and `analysis-report` on Mondays at 06:20 UTC. All three read `ORMA_MATERIALISE_SECRET_KEY` from Vault, which is now set.
- **Telegram.** The Login Widget works on `orma.nryn.dev`. BotFather's `/setdomain` for `@orma_tele_bot` is set to that domain. A bot has one login domain, so `localhost` always shows "Bot domain invalid".
- **P9 is in motion.** The UI is being rebuilt as a phone-first product UI. T8.4 records after P9 deploys. Screenshots in T8.3 wait for it too.
- **Fixtures.** The conversation in `testdata/calle/` is synthetic, as `testdata/calle/README.md` explains. Provider summary and evidence text there still names the operator.
- **Nothing in P8 exists yet.** There is no root `README.md`, no `scripts/seed.ts`, and `.github/workflows/` holds only `_env-example.yml`.

## Rules for every P8 task

**No calls.** Nothing in P8 places a real call. There is no live call run, and the demo exchange is synthetic.

**Check dry run before touching production.** `ORMA_DRY_RUN` is a function secret whose value cannot be read back. A profile with a confirmed phone, live consent and an active slot gets dialled by `tick` for real if dry run is off. Before any production write, the operator confirms `ORMA_DRY_RUN=true` by setting it again with `supabase secrets set`. Say in the review file that this happened.

**Production writes need the operator.** Build and test against `scripts/p6-local-stack.sh`. Running against the linked project, opening the pull request, uploading the video, and submitting Devpost or the survey all wait for the operator's explicit go-ahead.

**Disclose, never disguise.** Seeded rows are marked and named. Synthetic audio is labelled on screen. The README, the video and the Devpost text say the same thing.

**Mask every number.** No real phone number, name of a third party, key or token appears in any file, screenshot, frame or log.

## Operator-only steps

| Step | For | When |
|---|---|---|
| Confirm `ORMA_DRY_RUN=true` in function secrets | T8.1, T8.4 | Before seeding production |
| Name the production account to seed | T8.1 | Before `--apply` |
| Create a private backup repository and a fine-grained token | T8.2 | Before the first scheduled run |
| Add the session pooler URL as a repository secret | T8.2 | Before the first scheduled run |
| Record the phone with scrcpy and upload publicly | T8.4 | After P9 deploys |
| Approve the fork, branch and pull request | T8.5 | After packaging passes review |
| Submit Devpost | T8.5 | Before submissions close |
| Submit the feedback survey | T8.6 | Before 18 September |

## Dates

Submissions close 14 September at 23:45 SGT, which is 21:15 IST. The feedback survey closes 18 September. Judging runs 30 September to 13 October. A free Supabase project pauses after seven days of low activity.

## Order

T8.1, T8.2, T8.3 and T8.6 share no files and start now. T8.4 needs T8.1 applied and P9 deployed. T8.5 needs T8.3 and T8.4.

---

### T8.1: Seed data and disclosure ★
```yaml
requires:   T1.1, T2.2
fixture-ok: yes
size:       S · frontier
owns:       scripts/seed.ts
status:     not-started
```
The demo needs history that no run of real calls produced, so the seed carries all of it.

**What the briefing needs.** `assemble_briefing` in `supabase/migrations/20260912160000_briefing.sql` counts every `item_mentions` row for an item. It ages an item from `since_date`, or from `created_at` when that is null, in the profile's timezone. It speaks "You've mentioned {text} {n} times." at three or more mentions and "It's been {n} days." at thirty or more. So the item text reads naturally after "mentioned", for example `the dentist`.

**What to seed, for one named account.**

- One item, `the dentist`, with `seeded = true`, `source = 'call'`, and `since_date` set to 34 days before the demo date in the profile's timezone.
- Three earlier call runs on three separate local dates, each `completed`, `answered_extracted`, `dry_run = true` and `billable = false`. Give each a stable idempotency key under `orma:seed:`, so a rerun changes nothing.
- One `item_mentions` row per seeded run for the item, each with an offset into that run's transcript.
- A synthetic `transcripts` row, a valid `results` row, and the `call_events` a dry-run run writes, for each seeded run. History, Patterns and Timeline then read coherently. Copy the shapes the dry-run dispatcher writes rather than inventing new ones.
- Optionally two or three more seeded items with fewer mentions, so Today does not look staged. Keep every one `seeded = true`.

**What not to seed.** Never a `scheduled` run, a slot, a consent row, a phone number or a pattern report. Seeded runs are terminal, so `tick` can never claim one. Patterns come from the real `analysis` function over the seeded rows, never from a hand-written report.

**The script.** Deno, run as `deno run scripts/seed.ts`. It reaches Supabase only through `ORMA_API_URL`, with `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, because the admin API rejects the new-format secret key.

- `--email <address>` names the account. Refuse if it has no `profiles` row.
- `--demo-date <YYYY-MM-DD>` fixes the date the 34 days count to. Default to today in the profile's zone.
- No flag prints the plan, with masked output, and writes nothing.
- `--apply` writes. `--remove` deletes every seeded row for that account and nothing else. That is the rollback.
- Refuse `--apply` against a non-local URL unless `--i-confirmed-dry-run` is also passed.

**Disclosure text.** Write the paragraph the README and the video both use. It names the seeded item, the seeded runs and their dates, and says they are dry-run rows that no call placed.

**Done when:** against the local stack, a plan run writes zero rows, `--apply` twice leaves the same row counts, `--remove` leaves zero seeded rows. `assemble_briefing` for that account returns "You've mentioned the dentist 3 times." and "It's been 34 days." from rows. Every seeded row is found by one query on `seeded` items or `orma:seed:` keys, and the disclosure paragraph exists.

---

### T8.2: Keepalive and backup
```yaml
requires:   T1.1
fixture-ok: yes
size:       S · mid
owns:       .github/workflows/keepalive.yml, scripts/restore-check.sh
status:     not-started
```
With no daily calls, nothing else keeps the project active through judging. A paused project stops `pg_cron` and takes the demo URL down before a judge opens it.

**One daily workflow, plus manual dispatch.**

1. **Activity.** A GET against PostgREST through `ORMA_API_URL`, with the publishable key as `apikey`. Fail the job on any status other than 200.
2. **Backup.** `pg_dump` with a Postgres 17 client, in custom format, pushed to the operator's private backup repository. Keep the newest 14 dumps and delete older ones.

**Reach the database through the session pooler.** `SUPABASE_DB_URL` points at the direct `db.<ref>` host. That host is IPv6 only on the free plan, and GitHub-hosted runners have no IPv6. The workflow reads a new secret, `SUPABASE_POOLER_URL`, the session-mode pooler string from the dashboard. It never prints it.

**Secrets and variables.** Copy the `env:` block from `.github/workflows/_env-example.yml` rather than writing one. Add only `SUPABASE_POOLER_URL`, `BACKUP_REPO` (a variable such as `nrynss/orma-backups`) and `BACKUP_REPO_TOKEN`. The token is fine-grained, with contents write on the backup repository only.

The dump holds phone numbers and consent rows, so it never lands in this repository, an artifact, or a log. Mask the job output.

**Restore check.** `scripts/restore-check.sh <dump>` restores a dump into a throwaway local Postgres 17 container and prints row counts per table. It never targets the linked project.

**Done when:** a manual dispatch passes both steps, the backup repository shows the dump, and `restore-check.sh` restores it locally with row counts matching production's own counts. After that, the workflow runs daily for a week and the project has not paused.

---

### T8.3: Submission README ★
```yaml
requires:   P2, P3, P4, P6, P7, soft P9
fixture-ok: yes
size:       M · frontier
owns:       README.md, docs/screens/
status:     not-started
```
The repository requires apps that place calls or create recurring jobs to document setup, side effects, cancellation, credential handling, and dry-run behaviour. All of it goes here. T8.5 adapts this file into the app README in the pull request, so write it to stand alone.

**Sections, in this order.**

1. **What Orma is.** One paragraph from `product.md` §1. The call arrives already knowing what you keep not doing.
2. **How the demo was made.** Seeded history from T8.1, named. A synthetic exchange, labelled. No live call run took place.
3. **Try it without calling anyone.** Clone, `scripts/p6-local-stack.sh up`, run the web app against it, sign in as the seed account, and watch a dry-run call reach a terminal state on Timeline. Then `down`.
4. **Architecture.** The two Workers, the Supabase functions table from `spec.md` §6, the three cron jobs, and one diagram of a call's life from `spec.md` §3.
5. **Deploy your own.** `scripts/bootstrap-env.sh`, the three places secrets live, `supabase db push`, `supabase functions deploy`, the Vault key, the Telegram webhook, BotFather `/setdomain`, Resend, and both `npm run deploy` commands. Each step names its command.
6. **Side effects.** A table of every effect and its trigger: phone calls, cron jobs, email, Telegram messages, stored voice notes, and CALL-E spend.
7. **Cancellation.** Cancel today's call, pause all calls, revoke consent, and delete the account from Settings. For an operator, unschedule each cron with `cron.unschedule`, and set dry run back on.
8. **Dry run.** `ORMA_DRY_RUN` defaults to true. `ORMA_DRY_RUN_FIXTURE` selects `completed`, `failed` or `no_result`. Say what a dry run writes to `call_events`. Turning it off places real calls at $0.05 each after 20 free.
9. **Credentials.** The publishable key is the only key in the bundle, and the build fails if a secret key appears under `web/`. List what each secret is for, by name only.
10. **Consent and numbers.** E.164 only. Consent is a row with the wording shown. Numbers are masked in every sample.
11. **Surfaces.** Web, Telegram and MCP, linking `docs/mcp.md`. Name Telegram's Bot API, CALL-E, Gemini on Vertex AI, Resend, Supabase and Cloudflare under third-party integrations.
12. **Known limitations.** Missed calls are not retried, per `product.md` §10. Calls arrive from a number you will not recognise and may be flagged as spam, per `feedback.md` issue 9.
13. **Screens.** Phone screenshots from P9 in `docs/screens/`, captured from the local stack with seeded data. Add these last.

Every command in the README is run at least once while writing it. Every sample number is masked or from a reserved fictional range.

**Done when:** a separate agent with no other context follows sections 3 and 7 on a clean clone and succeeds. The review confirms every command runs, every side effect in the code is in the table, and no secret value or real number appears.

---

### T8.4: Demo video ★
```yaml
requires:   T8.1, T6.6, T6.8, P9
fixture-ok: yes
size:       L · frontier
owns:       dev-diary/demo-video.md
status:     not-started
```
Under three minutes, public on YouTube or Vimeo. The operator records the phone with scrcpy. An agent writes the script, the shot list and the synthetic audio plan in `dev-diary/demo-video.md`, and reviews the cut against it.

**The centre is one exchange, not a feature tour.**

> **Orma:** You've mentioned the dentist three times. It's been 34 days.
> **User:** Kill it.
> **Orma:** Done. It's gone.

That beat carries give-before-take and unpunished quitting together. Lead with the call arriving already knowing, not with scheduling. The list repository already ships a scheduler wrapper for reminders, so that ground is taken.

**The exchange is synthetic, and the video says so on screen.** Render both voices with a text-to-speech engine. Hold a caption such as "Synthetic voices. No real call." for the whole exchange. Never imply that a real person took a call or that the audio is a recording.

**Shot list, roughly.**

1. The synthetic exchange over the landing page's call beat, captioned.
2. Today on the phone, with the dentist item showing three mentions and 34 days from rows. Caption it as seeded.
3. Items, retiring the dentist with one tap. The list updates in place.
4. Timeline, showing a dry-run run, labelled dry run. If the next briefing is shown, schedule that dry-run run after the retirement, so its briefing no longer names the item.
5. Patterns, the report prose beside its facts.
6. Telegram on the same phone, a captured item and its receipt.
7. Settings, showing cancel today, pause and delete.
8. A closing card with the seed disclosure, the synthetic label and the repository link.

**Recording.** Check `ORMA_DRY_RUN=true` first. Use `scrcpy --record` at the phone's native resolution. Turn on do not disturb so no notification lands in the frame. The incoming call screen never appears, because there is no call, and nothing may stage a saved contact.

**Done when:** `demo-video.md` holds the final script with timings under three minutes, every caption is legible at phone size, every number shown comes from seeded rows, the video is public, and its link is in `demo-video.md`.

**The pull request carries the app itself.** Orma's own repository is private, so the PR is the public code. Recent app PRs to that repository ship full source.

Read `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `docs/community-review-policy.md`, `docs/git-naming-conventions.md` and the pull request template in that repository first. They change, and the review checks them as they are on the day.

**Package with a script.** `scripts/package-list-pr.sh <target-dir>` copies a clean tree into `apps/web/orma/` of a local checkout of the list repository, so every run produces the same result.

- **Include.** `web/`, `supabase/`, `proxy/`, `scripts/`, `testdata/`, `docs/`, `.env.example`, and an app `README.md` adapted from T8.3.
- **Exclude.** `dev-diary/`, `design/`, `AGENTS.md`, agent configs, every `.env`, `node_modules`, build output, and anything gitignored.
- **Replace in the copy.** The `summary`, `evidence` and task text in `testdata/calle/` and in the inline fixture in `dispatch-mode.ts` still carry provider text that names the operator. Replace them with synthetic text in the packaged copy. Rerun the Deno tests inside the copy afterwards.
- **Scan the copy.** Fail on any phone-shaped string outside reserved fictional ranges, any key-shaped string, the operator's name, and any `supabase.co` project host.
- **Index.** Add one row for Orma to `apps/README.md`, in that table's format and tone.

**The list repository's review policy.** An app that needs private services must have a no-call path. The first run path in the app README is the local stack in dry run. Hosted Supabase and live CALL-E come after it, as opt-in steps. Real test-call artifacts and private transcripts are Must Fix.

**Their naming and checks.** Branch in `<type>/<short-kebab-summary>` form, such as `feat/orma-accountability-calls`. PR title `feat(apps): add Orma accountability calls`, or similar in their format. Fill in every item of their pull request template. Run `python3 scripts/validate_repository.py` in the checkout and pass it. English only.

**Devpost.** The description carries the same disclosure as the README: seeded history and a synthetic exchange. Judging covers real world impact, quality of the idea, technical implementation, and product experience and demo, per `product.md` §9.

The fixture conversation is now synthetic and the P8 doc is rewritten so each task can go straight to an agent. Both are committed as `7dd77df` on top of `8dac5a3`, neither pushed. The other session's uncommitted P9 work is untouched. I checked `/login` after your BotFather change and the Telegram button is there.

**Synthetic transcript**
- **Where:** the real call's words are replaced in every copy:
  - `transcript.json`
  - the same turns inside `call-completed.json`
  - the per-turn messages in `call-completed-events.json`
  - the inline copy in `supabase/functions/_shared/dispatch-mode.ts`
- **What stayed:** speakers, turn count and timings, plus "Continental" at 0:44. Everything the tests check still holds. The product line "You've mentioned the dentist three times. It's been 34 days." is kept.
- **Test pin:** one test in `calle.ts` pins a SHA-256 digest of the completed fixture, so it caught the change. I updated the pin. This commit is the review record for that change, since `calle.ts` belongs to T2.4.
- **Tests:** all eight suites that use these files pass with the same counts as before: dispatch-mode 13, finalise 88, ingest 15, poll 21, calle 50, receipt 5, tick 101, deliver-telegram 10.
- **Housekeeping:** I removed the `.gitignore` entry because the file is safe to track now. I also added `testdata/calle/README.md` saying the conversation is synthetic.
- **Still real:** the `summary`, `evidence` and task text in those files are still CALL-E's output from the real call and name you. T8.5 replaces them in the pull request copy.

**`PHASE-8-ship.md`: what each agent gets**
- **Current state:** what's live, the three crons, Telegram working, P9 in progress, the synthetic fixtures, and that none of P8 exists yet.
- **Rules:** no calls, and confirm dry run is on before touching production. Production writes, the pull request, uploads and submissions wait for you. Disclose everything and mask every number.
- **Your steps:**
  - confirm dry run is on;
  - name the account to seed;
  - create the backup repository, a token for it and the pooler URL secret;
  - record with scrcpy;
  - approve the pull request;
  - submit Devpost and the survey.
- **Order:** T8.1, T8.2, T8.3 and T8.6 start now. T8.4 waits for the seed and P9. T8.5 waits for T8.3 and T8.4.

**What each task now spells out**
- **T8.1 Seed:** what `assemble_briefing` needs to say "3 times" and "34 days". It lists exactly which rows to create and never to create. It also sets how the script is run: a plan by default, `--apply`, `--remove` to roll back, and a dry-run confirmation flag for production.
- **T8.2 Keepalive:** your `SUPABASE_DB_URL` points at the direct database host. That host is IPv6-only on the free plan, and GitHub's runners have no IPv6, so the workflow needs a new `SUPABASE_POOLER_URL` secret. The backups keep 14 dumps in a private repository, with a local-only restore check.
- **T8.3 README:** 13 sections in order, and it's done only when a fresh agent can follow it on a clean clone.
- **T8.4 Video:** the agent writes the script and shot list, and you record with scrcpy. The voices are synthetic and captioned. Every number shown comes from seeded rows.

# T8.1 round 1 review

- Reviewer: RevT81R1 (orchestrator session, did not implement)
- Date: 2026-09-14
- Subject: uncommitted `scripts/seed.ts` on `main` at `7dd77df`, 1002 lines
- Specification: the T8.1 block in `dev-diary/PHASE-8-ship.md`

## Verdict

**REMEDIATE**

| C | H | M | L |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 | 2 | 2 |

The done-when list holds on the local stack. Two defects break what the seed exists for. A rerun undoes the demo's live retirement and deletes real mentions. The seeded history is too sparse for the analysis function, so Patterns has nothing to show.

## Scope

`git status` shows `scripts/seed.ts` as the only new T8.1 path. The phase doc status line reads `claimed:t8.1-impl`. No review file existed before this one. I read the whole script, the T8.1 block, `assemble_briefing`, `compute_pattern_facts`, the `analysis` report window, and the dry-run dispatcher. I changed no code.

## Independent evidence

Every measurement below is my own run against `scripts/p6-local-stack.sh` (API on 58321), account `local@example.com`, `--demo-date 2026-09-14`. Counts are for that account. The stack was torn down afterwards, and zero `orma-p6-local` containers remain.

1. **Baseline.** items 4, runs 6, mentions 3, events 2, transcripts 1, results 1, slots 1, consents 1, scheduled 1.
2. **Plan run.** Exit 0. Every count unchanged.
3. **First `--apply`.** items 7, runs 9 (3 with `orma:seed:` keys), mentions 8, events 11, transcripts 4, results 4. Slots, consents and scheduled runs unchanged at 1, 1 and 1.
4. **Second `--apply`.** Identical counts. The `call_events` ids changed, because the script deletes and reinserts them.
5. **Briefing.** `assemble_briefing(user, '08:00', '2026-09-14 09:00+05:30')` lead line reads "You've mentioned the dentist 3 times. It's been 34 days." The script's own check printed both ticks.
6. **Seeded runs.** 2026-08-17 `ok`, 2026-08-31 `ok`, 2026-09-11 `unknown`. All `completed`, `dry_run = true`, `terminal_writer = dry_run`.
7. **Non-local guard.** `ORMA_API_URL=https://orma-api.nryn.dev` with `--apply` and no confirmation flag exits 1 before any request.
8. **`--remove`.** Every count returns to the baseline in item 1. Zero seeded items remain. The T1.6 seed rows survive.

## Findings

The PR itself can be a single command. Most of the prep can happen now, while P9 and T8.1 finish. Nothing for the PR exists yet: no packaging script, no root README, no fork. I cloned the CALL-E list repo read-only and read its rules. Their validator passes on their current `main`, and their CI runs only that validator on PRs.

**Fix before the PR**
1. **The Devpost draft makes a false claim.** `devpost-submission.md` says "The demo records a real Orma call." The exchange is synthetic, by your decision and in T6.8 and T8.4. Their policy blocks "materially false claims", and Devpost judges read the same text. That line needs rewriting.
2. **Anyone can make Orma call any number.** Onboarding marks a typed-in number as confirmed without checking it, and your live demo is open to sign-ups. So if production dry run is ever off, a stranger could have Orma call someone else's phone every day. Their policy treats "unauthorized live destinations" as a merge blocker. The simplest answer is to keep `ORMA_DRY_RUN=true` on the hosted demo and say so in the README. Number verification is the heavier fix.
3. **Orma calls on a schedule, with no per-call confirmation.** For live-capable hackathon demos their policy asks for "explicit per-run operator intent". Orma's opt-in is the consent row, the time slot the user picked, and dry run being on by default. The policy accepts a local operator's attestation, so the README should state that framing plainly, with cancel and pause next to it. This is a review risk rather than something to change in code.

**What the package would need to clean up**
I scanned the files the PR would copy: `web`, `supabase`, `proxy`, `scripts`, `testdata`, `docs` and `.env.example`, about 160 tracked files.
- **Your name** appears in 6 files: `briefing.ts`, `calle.ts`, `dispatch-mode.ts`, `tick/index.ts`, `call-completed.json`, and the `/dev/ui` gallery page. Replace it in the copy.
- **Phone-shaped test numbers** such as `+9199…` aren't in reserved fictional ranges. Their policy only prefers reserved ranges, but swapping them is cheap. Switch to `+1 555 01xx`, then rerun the tests inside the copy.
- **`orma.nryn.dev`** appears in 34 files, and your Supabase project ref in 8, including `proxy/wrangler.jsonc` and `web/package.json`. Neither is a secret, and the live demo URL is fine to publish. For an app others can deploy, they should be settings, or at least called out in the README. This needs your call.
- **`proxy/worker-configuration.d.ts`** is 590 KB of Wrangler-generated types. Leave it out and document `npm run cf-typegen`.
- **Passes their checks already:** no `file:` or `workspace:` dependencies, no Chinese, Japanese or Korean text (the Malayalam is fine), and no old repo name. Their trailing-whitespace check only covers one Dify template.

**Build now, as T8.5 prep with no fork and no PR yet**
- **`scripts/package-list-pr.sh`:**
  1. copy the clean tree into `apps/web/orma/` of a scratch clone;
  2. apply the replacements above;
  3. scan for numbers, names, keys and `supabase.co` hosts;
  4. run the Deno tests and `npm run check` inside the copy;
  5. run their `validate_repository.py`.
- **A ready-to-paste PR body:** their template with every checklist item answered.
- **The `apps/README.md` row:** in their table's tone.
- **The Devpost disclosure paragraph:** matching the README.

**Waiting on other work**
- **T8.3, the root README.** It becomes the app README in the PR and is the biggest remaining piece. It can be written now, with screenshots added after P9.
- **T8.1 approved.** The README uses its disclosure paragraph, and the Devpost text should match it.
- **P9 landed.** The PR is a snapshot of the code, so package after the UI is final.
- **The public video URL.** Devpost needs it and the PR URL. I didn't find the video script in the repo, so keep it wherever it lives now.

**Needs your OK on the day**
Create the fork `nrynss/awesome-phone-call-agents`. Run the packaging script, push the branch `feat/orma-accountability-calls`, and open the PR titled `feat(apps): add Orma accountability calls` with the prepared body. Then paste the PR URL into Devpost and submit.

You're right on all four points, and I had the call wrong. The Devpost line "The demo records a real Orma call. The on-screen history is seeded dry-run data" was accurate, so there's nothing to fix there. I've corrected my notes and the P8 doc to match.

**Why your name appears.** Only in test data and sample values, never in anything the app sends or shows to users:
- **The T1.4 fixtures** (`call-completed.json` and the copy inside `dispatch-mode.ts`): CALL-E's own summary and evidence from your test call, such as "The call connected with Narayan…", plus the task text "calling Narayan".
- **Test stubs** in `calle.ts`, `tick/index.ts` and `briefing.ts` that fake a briefing with `user_name: "Narayan"`.
- **One placeholder** in the `/dev/ui` component gallery, which is development-only.

It's your own name, which their policy allows. The fixtures are still CALL-E's output from a real call, though, so the package script should swap the name for a neutral one in the copy.

**Phone-shaped strings aren't an issue.** I checked the files against your real number from `.env`, and it appears in none of them. Every match is an obvious test value like `+9199…99`, `+1555…00` or `+1415…71`. Their policy calls these a minor, non-blocking fix at most, so the script can leave them alone.

**`orma.nryn.dev` isn't an issue.** It's the project's name and live URL, and it stays.

**The proxy is left out by the script.** I updated T8.5 so `scripts/package-list-pr.sh` excludes `proxy/` itself. One consequence to plan for: the web app and several functions refuse any API URL containing `supabase.co` (starting at `web/src/lib/supabase.ts:23`). That guard exists because your network can't reach Supabase's hosts directly, which is why the proxy exists. Someone deploying the packaged app without the proxy can't point it straight at their Supabase project. Either the README explains a way round it, or that guard changes first.

**What I changed in `PHASE-8-ship.md`**
- **Rules:** P8's rules now say real calls over seeded history, and that Orma is open to anyone who signs up and consents. No agent places a call while building or reviewing.
- **Dry run:** you state production's mode before seeding, and turn it off only for the recording window.
- **T8.4:** now a real call on your phone.
  - The briefing reads the seeded rows, and "Kill it" retires the item through the real ingest.
  - The shot list covers the call, Today, History, Timeline, Patterns, Telegram and Settings.
  - The history is captioned as seeded, never the call, and there's a retake plan if the model misses the beat.
- **T8.3 and T8.5:** the disclosure is now "a real call over seeded history".

Those doc edits aren't committed. The same file has another agent's uncommitted changes (the T8.1 status line and a new Devpost line), and a commit would sweep those in.

**One thing still worth deciding now that Orma is open.** Onboarding accepts whatever number someone types and marks it confirmed. With dry run off, a stranger could sign up with someone else's number, and Orma would call that person daily. Their policy counts unauthorized call destinations as a merge blocker. The fix could be number confirmation before the first call, or a README statement of what the consent step covers and what it doesn't.

content.text:
A number would count as confirmed only once the person who picks up that phone proves they signed up. Two changes make that true: the database stops letting users set "confirmed" themselves, and something other than the user proves the number.

**What happens today**
- **The browser marks the number confirmed.** Onboarding saves the typed number and sets `phone_confirmed_at` in the same step (`web/src/routes/app/onboarding/submit.ts:152`).
- **Users can write that field directly.** The `profiles` security policy lets a signed-in user update any column of their own row. Even with the UI fixed, anyone could set `phone_confirmed_at` with one API request.
- **The dispatcher checks the right thing.** It already refuses any call without `phone_confirmed_at` (`supabase/functions/_shared/calle.ts:339`). Once only the server can set that field, every other call path is covered too.

**Step 1: only the server can confirm a number (required whichever option you pick)**
A migration that:
- stops signed-in users writing `phone_confirmed_at`;
- clears `phone_confirmed_at` whenever `phone_e164` changes, so switching to a new number means confirming again;
- stops onboarding and Settings sending that field.

After this, onboarding saves the number, the account shows "Number not confirmed" (Today's blocked state already exists), and no scheduled call is placed.

**Step 2: how the number gets confirmed**

| Option | How it works | Cost and reach | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Telegram contact share** | In Telegram, the user taps "Share my number". Telegram sends the bot the number on that Telegram account, with the sender's own id. If the id matches the user's linked Telegram account and the number matches `phone_e164`, the server sets `phone_confirmed_at`. | Free and instant, with no new provider. Telegram linking already exists. | Only for Telegram users. The bot is currently "receipts only, never prompts" (spec §8), so this needs a small contract change. |
| **B. A short confirmation call with a code** | The app shows a 4-digit code and asks CALL-E to place one short call. The call states that someone signed this number up for Orma and asks for the code. The code is extracted with a result schema. A match confirms the number. A miss, no answer or a refusal confirms nothing and never redials. | About $0.05 per attempt. Works for everyone. Uses only CALL-E, which also suits the hackathon. | The number still gets one call. Holding the code proves the caller has the phone. Limits are needed, such as one attempt per number per day and three per account. |
| **C. SMS code** | A standard one-time code by text message. | Adds a new provider, and India requires sender registration (DLT) first. | Outside the frozen stack. Not recommended. |

**My recommendation: A plus B.**
- Telegram users confirm for free through A.
- Email-only users get the confirmation call through B.

Their review policy accepts a single call that discloses itself, asks for proof and never repeats, as standard voice verification. What it blocks is repeated unauthorized calls, and Step 1 plus the dispatcher gate rules those out.

**What it would take as tasks**
1. **Lock confirmation to the server** (Step 1). A migration plus onboarding and Settings edits. It has to land first and needs the most careful review.
2. **Telegram contact confirmation** (option A). The `telegram` function handles a shared contact, and Settings adds a "Confirm with Telegram" step.
3. **Confirmation call** (option B):
   - a separate call task and result schema in `calle.ts`;
   - a function or RPC that starts the call, rate-limited per number and account;
   - the code shown in onboarding and Settings.

   Its ingest sets `phone_confirmed_at` only when the extracted code matches.
4. **Copy and docs.** Onboarding currently says "Saving still sets the confirmed timestamp", and that becomes false. The README explains the confirmation steps for the list repository's reviewers.

Task 3 touches the call engine, which is the most sensitive code in the repo. Tasks 1 and 2 are small.

Should I add these as tasks? The options are a P6 follow-up or a short new phase, with A only or A plus B.
Only B is needed. Telegram is just decoration.
Option B it is. Before writing the phase I'm checking how the webhook treats calls that aren't daily call runs, and what else can change a user's number.

# P10: Number confirmation

```yaml
id:       P10
size:     M
requires: [P2, P5, P6]
blocks:   [T8.4, T8.5]
parallel: [P9, P8 except T8.4 and T8.5]
```

**Goal:** Orma calls a number every day only after the person holding that phone has proved they signed up. Anyone can use Orma, so nobody can sign up somebody else's number.

**Why now.** Onboarding saves a typed number and sets `phone_confirmed_at` in the same browser request (`web/src/routes/app/onboarding/submit.ts:152`). The `profiles_owner` policy lets a signed-in user write every column of their own row, so one PostgREST request can set it too. With dry run off, a stranger could sign up with a third party's number and have it rung daily.

The CALL-E list repository's review policy names unauthorized live destinations as a merge blocker. T8.5 cannot open its pull request until this phase closes, and T8.4 records its real call through the new flow.

**The mechanism, decided 14 September.** A one-time confirmation call reads a short code aloud. The user types that code into Orma. Only the person holding the phone hears it, so a correct code proves possession. The server generates and checks the code. No model ever produces or judges it.

**What stays true.** The dispatcher already refuses any run without `phone_confirmed_at` (`supabase/functions/_shared/calle.ts:339`). P10 does not change that gate. It changes who may set the field. Every call path, including materialise, tick and MCP, is covered through that one check.

### T10.1: Confirmation belongs to the server ★

owns:       supabase/migrations/<timestamp>_phone_confirmation_guard.sql, web/src/routes/app/onboarding/submit.ts, web/src/routes/app/onboarding/check.ts, web/src/lib/database.types.ts, supabase/functions/_shared/database.types.ts

**The guard.** A `before insert or update` trigger on `profiles`. For any caller that is not the service role, it forces `phone_confirmed_at` to null on insert. On update it keeps the old value when `phone_e164` is unchanged, and clears it when the number changes. A trigger holds even if a later policy or grant widens access, which a column grant alone does not.

### T10.2: Confirmation call and code check ★
```yaml
requires:   T10.1, T2.4, T2.6
fixture-ok: yes
size:       M · frontier
owns:       supabase/migrations/<timestamp>_phone_confirmations.sql, supabase/functions/confirm-phone/, supabase/functions/_shared/calle.ts (confirmation request only), supabase/functions/calle-webhook/index.ts (routing only), supabase/config.toml ([functions.confirm-phone] only), web/src/lib/database.types.ts, supabase/functions/_shared/database.types.ts
status:     not-started
```
One call reads a code. One function checks it. Nothing else can confirm a number.

**Table.** `phone_confirmations`: id, user_id, phone_e164, code_hash, attempts, state (`requested`, `dialled`, `refused`, `failed`, `confirmed`, `expired`), idempotency_key unique, calle_call_id, created_at, expires_at, confirmed_at. RLS lets the owner read state and timestamps only. The owner never reads `code_hash`. Only the service role writes.

**Start: `POST /functions/v1/confirm-phone`.** The caller's JWT identifies the user. It takes no user id and no number.

1. Refuse unless the profile has an E.164 number, the number is not already confirmed, and a live `outbound_calls` consent exists.
2. Enforce limits before any call. At most one attempt per account every ten minutes, three per account per day, and five per number per day across all accounts.
3. Generate a six-digit code with a cryptographic random source. Store only a salted hash. Expire it after ten minutes.
4. Insert the row, then place exactly one call through `calle.ts`, which stays the only module that can POST `/v1/calls`. The idempotency key is `orma:confirm:<row id>`. A retried request with the same row returns its state and places no second call.
5. Never retry a failed, unanswered or refused call. The user asks again, inside the limits.

**The call.** A separate task text and a minimal result schema in `calle.ts`. The call says it is Orma, that someone asked Orma to call this number, and reads the code digit by digit, twice. It says that if you did not ask for this, hang up and Orma will not call again. Set `metadata.phone_confirmation_id`, not `call_run_id`. It asks nothing and captures nothing.

**Dry run.** With `ORMA_DRY_RUN=true`, no call is placed. The function records the masked request. When `ORMA_ENV` is not production, it also returns the code in the response so local tests can complete. In production it never returns the code.

**Check: `verify_phone_code(code text)`.** A `security definer` RPC for `authenticated` only, revoked from `public` and `anon`. It acts on `auth.uid()`. It compares against the newest unexpired row whose number still equals the profile's number. After five wrong codes the row expires. A match sets the row `confirmed` and sets `profiles.phone_confirmed_at`, which the T10.1 guard allows for this definer.

**Webhook.** `calle-webhook` currently requires `metadata.call_run_id`. Route events that carry `metadata.phone_confirmation_id` to update that row's state only. They never touch `call_runs`, never ingest, and never error in a way that makes CALL-E retry forever. Keep de-duplication by event id.

Record any CALL-E friction in `dev-diary/feedback.md` in the same session, per `AGENTS.md`.

**Done when:** on the local stack in dry run, start then verify confirms the number, and each of these holds.

- A wrong code five times expires the row, and no code confirms a changed number.
- The limits refuse a fourth attempt in a day and a second within ten minutes.
- A second user cannot read or verify the first user's row.
- The same start request twice places one call.
- A webhook event for a confirmation call changes no `call_runs` row.
- No response or log in production mode contains the code.

A live pin is evidence, never a gate: the operator runs one real confirmation call to their own number and records the response shape.

| **T10.1 ★** | Only the server can mark a number confirmed. A database trigger ignores any attempt by a user to set `phone_confirmed_at`, and clears it whenever the number changes. Onboarding stops sending the field. | A migration, `submit.ts`, `check.ts`, types |

- **Before calling:** the account must have live consent.
- **Limits:**
  - at most one attempt every 10 minutes per account;

- **One call per request:** each attempt has its own idempotency key, so retrying a request never places a second call.

- **The code:** stored only as a salted hash, and it expires after 10 minutes or 5 wrong tries.
- **What the call says:** "if you didn't ask for this, hang up, and Orma won't call again."
- **Webhook:** events for confirmation calls never touch `call_runs`.

10 A daily two-minute accountability call. It remembers what you keep not doing. 11

12 13 ## What Orma is 14 15 Orma is a daily two-minute accountability call. It rings at a time you chose, leads with what you keep not doing, asks what needs capturing, and hangs up. The thesis is accountability, not reminding. An app notification gets dismissed without consequence or witness. A spoken question, asked by a machine that remembers what you said last time, carries weight. Orma treats being a known machine as an asset. You speak honestly because no human feels disappointed when you admit inaction. 16 17 ## How the demo was made 18 19 The call in the demo video is a real phone call. CALL-E dials the operator's phone on a real slot, and the operator answers. 20 21 The history that the call reads is seeded data. The script `scripts/seed.ts` creates these historical rows without placing phone calls. It seeds the item "the dentist" with `seeded = true`, `source = 'call'`, and a `since_date` 34 days before the demo date. It writes three completed call runs with `dry_run = true` and `billable = false`. Each run carries a stable idempotency key under the `orma:seed:` prefix, synthetic transcript turns, and validated structured results. One `item_mentions` row per run links "the dentist" to that run's transcript offset. The seed also adds two items, "renew the passport" and "weekend groceries", so the Today screen looks natural. 22 23 When the database function `assemble_briefing` runs, SQL aggregates these rows into the briefing. The call speaks: "You've mentioned the dentist 3 times. It's been 34 days." The prompt never invents these numbers. A single query matching `seeded = true` or `orma:seed:%` identifies every seeded row. 24 25 ## Try it without calling anyone 26 27 You can explore the full application locally with Docker and dry-run fixtures. This flow places no outbound phone calls and spends no money. 28 29 1. Clone the repository and enter the directory: 30 31 ```bash 32 git clone https://github.com/nrynss/orma.git 33 cd orma 34 ``` 35 36 2. Start the local Supabase stack: 37 38 ```bash 39 ./scripts/p6-local-stack.sh up 40 ``` 41 42 This command starts a local Supabase stack in Docker, runs migrations, and inserts local harness rows. It creates three test accounts, all with password `local-dev-password`: 43 - `local@example.com` has seeded history, an answered call, and a scheduled run. 44 - `firstrun@example.com` has a fresh profile with zero calls. 45 - `live@example.com` has a call run in the `awaiting_result` state. 46 47 3. Start the web application in a new terminal: 48 49 ```bash 50 cd web && env $(../scripts/p6-local-stack.sh env) npm run dev 51 ``` 52 53 4. Open `http://localhost:5173` in your browser. Sign in as `local@example.com` with password `local-dev-password`. 54 55 5. Navigate to `http://localhost:5173/app/timeline`. Watch the simulated call advance through dispatch, polling, and finalisation into a terminal state (`completed` or `answered_extracted`). 56 57 6. When finished, stop the local stack: 58 59 ```bash 60 ./scripts/p6-local-stack.sh down 61 ``` 62 63 ## Architecture 64 65 Orma uses a serverless and edge architecture without persistent daemon processes. 66 67 ### Cloudflare Workers 68 69 Orma deploys two Cloudflare Workers: 70 - `web/` serves `orma.nryn.dev`. It runs SvelteKit with the Cloudflare adapter and binds static assets. 71 - `proxy/` serves `orma-api.nryn.dev`. It acts as a reverse proxy to Supabase PostgREST and Edge Functions, keeping DNS hostnames single-level and insulating clients from upstream host changes. 72 73 ### Supabase Edge Functions 74 75 All backend endpoints run on Supabase Edge Functions in Deno: 76 77 | Function | Trigger | Description | 78 |---|---|---| 79 | `tick` | `pg_cron`, every minute | Claims scheduled runs, dispatches outbound calls, polls awaiting calls, and finalises completed runs | 80 | `materialise` | `pg_cron`, nightly at 00:10 UTC | Generates call runs for the next 48 hours from active user slots | 81 | `calle-webhook` | CALL-E HTTP POST | Validates webhook secret, de-duplicates event IDs, re-fetches authoritative runs, and ingests results | 82 | `telegram` | Telegram webhook | Captures text items and audio voice notes, transcribes voice with Gemini, and delivers post-call receipts | 83 | `mcp` | MCP client requests | Exposes Model Context Protocol tools over streamable HTTP under user JWT authentication | 84 | `auth-telegram` | Browser client | Verifies Telegram Login Widget HMAC signature and mints user auth tokens | 85 | `analysis` | `pg_cron`, weekly | Computes aggregate behavioral facts in SQL, phrases pattern reports with Gemini, and delivers them | 86 87 ### Cron jobs 88 89 Three `pg_cron` schedules drive background operations: 90 - `tick`: Runs every minute (`* * * * *`). It claims due runs via `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, dispatches CALL-E requests, and advances the call state machine. 91 - `materialise`: Runs daily at 00:10 UTC (`10 0 * * *`). It reads active slots and inserts upcoming `call_runs` in the user's local timezone. 92 - `analysis`: Runs every Sunday at midnight UTC (`0 0 * * 0`). It aggregates weekly call metrics into `pattern_reports.facts` and generates natural-language insights. 93 94 ### Call run lifecycle 95 96 ```text 97 scheduled ──claim──► claimed ──dispatch──► dispatched 98 │ │ 99 │ ▼ 100 │ awaiting_result 101 │ │ │ │ 102 ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ 103 canceled completed no_result failed 104 ``` 105 106 A call run transitions through explicit states: 107 - `scheduled`: Created by `materialise` for a future slot. 108 - `claimed`: Locked by `tick` using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to prevent duplicate dialing. 109 - `dispatched`: Sent to CALL-E with a unique idempotency key (`orma:{user_id}:{local_date}:{part_of_day}:v1`). 110 - `awaiting_result`: Awaiting webhook delivery or polling reconciliation. 111 - `completed`: Successfully answered and processed. It receives disposition `answered_extracted` or `answered_no_result`. 112 - `failed`: The recipient did not answer or the provider reported an error. It receives disposition `not_answered`. 113 - `canceled`: Canceled by user request before dispatch. 114 115 ## Deploy your own 116 117 Follow these steps to deploy Orma to your own Supabase, Cloudflare, and CALL-E accounts. 118 119 ### 1. Configure environment and secrets 120 121 Orma manages secrets across three distinct locations: 122 - Local `.env` file: Used for local scripts and tests. You generate it with `scripts/bootstrap-env.sh`. 123 - GitHub repository secrets and variables: Used by CI workflows to build and test code without exposing credentials. 124 - Supabase function secrets: Read by deployed Edge Functions in production. 125 126 Generate your local `.env` by exporting required values and running: 127 128 ```bash 129 ./scripts/bootstrap-env.sh 130 ``` 131 132 ### 2. Push database schema 133 134 Apply migrations to your Supabase project: 135 136 ```bash 137 supabase db push 138 ``` 139 140 ### 3. Deploy Supabase Edge Functions 141 142 Deploy all serverless functions: 143 144 ```bash 145 supabase functions deploy 146 ``` 147 148 ### 4. Store the Vault encryption key 149 150 Set the encryption key for sensitive tokens in Supabase secrets: 151 152 ```bash 153 supabase secrets set ORMA_VAULT_KEY="" 154 ``` 155 156 ### 5. Set up the Telegram webhook 157 158 Register your deployed function URL with the Telegram Bot API: 159 160 ```bash 161 curl -sS -X POST "https://api.telegram.org/bot${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}/setWebhook" \ 162 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 163 -d '{"url":"https://orma-api.nryn.dev/functions/v1/telegram","secret_token":"'"${TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET}"'"}' 164 ``` 165 166 ### 6. Configure Telegram bot domain 167 168 Open Telegram and message `@BotFather`. Send `/setdomain`, pick your bot, and enter your domain `orma.nryn.dev`. 169 170 ### 7. Configure Resend email delivery 171 172 Set your Resend API credentials in Supabase function secrets: 173 174 ```bash 175 supabase secrets set RESEND_API_KEY="" RESEND_FROM="Orma " 176 ``` 177 178 ### 8. Deploy Cloudflare Workers 179 180 Deploy the web application: 181 182 ```bash 183 cd web && npm run deploy 184 ``` 185 186 Deploy the API proxy: 187 188 ```bash 189 cd proxy && npm run deploy 190 ``` 191 192 ## Side effects 193 194 Orma executes explicit external operations. The table below lists every side effect and its trigger: 195 196 | Effect | Trigger | Target | Cost or Retention | 197 |---|---|---|---| 198 | Phone call | Active slot during `tick` cron run | Callee phone number | Consumes CALL-E balance ($0.05 per call after 20 free) | 199 | Cron materialisation | `pg_cron` schedule at 00:10 UTC | `call_runs` table | Database row writes | 200 | Cron tick dispatch | `pg_cron` schedule every minute | Supabase Edge Functions | Function invocations | 201 | Cron analysis | `pg_cron` schedule weekly on Sunday | `pattern_reports` table | Vertex AI Gemini token usage | 202 | Magic link email | User requests email sign-in | User email address | Resend API email delivery | 203 | Email receipt | Completed call with email receipt enabled | User email address | Resend API email delivery | 204 | Telegram receipt | Completed call with Telegram receipt enabled | User Telegram chat | Free Telegram Bot API message | 205 | Telegram pattern report | Completed weekly analysis report | User Telegram chat | Free Telegram Bot API message | 206 | Stored voice note | User uploads audio note in Telegram | Ephemeral buffer | Processed by Gemini and deleted | 207 | CALL-E spend | Each outbound call request | CALL-E account | \$0.05 per call after 20 free calls | 208 209 ## Cancellation 210 211 Users and operators have full control over stopping calls and removing data. 212 213 ### User cancellation (Settings page) 214 215 Users can manage or terminate calls from `https://orma.nryn.dev/app/settings`: 216 - **Cancel today's call**: Cancels today's scheduled run immediately. The system updates the run state to `canceled` and dials no call today. Tomorrow's call remains scheduled. 217 - **Pause all calls**: Disables active slots. The materialiser schedules no new runs until the user resumes calls. 218 - **Revoke consent**: Sets `revoked_at` on the user's `outbound_calls` consent row. The dispatcher refuses to place calls to profiles without active consent. 219 - **Delete account**: Purges the profile and cascades deletion across all slots, items, mentions, transcripts, call runs, and deliveries. 220 221 ### Operator cancellation 222 223 An operator can halt all platform calls and recurring jobs directly: 224 225 1. Unschedule cron jobs in SQL: 226 227 ```sql 228 select cron.unschedule('orma-tick') 229 select cron.unschedule('orma-materialise') 230 select cron.unschedule('orma-analysis') 231 ``` 232 233 2. Re-enable dry-run mode in Supabase secrets so no real calls go out: 234 235 ```bash 236 supabase secrets set ORMA_DRY_RUN=true 237 ``` 238 239 ## Dry run 240 241 Orma enforces dry run mode by default. Developers opt into spending, never out of it. 242 243 The environment variable `ORMA_DRY_RUN` defaults to `true`. While set to `true`, the dispatcher never contacts the CALL-E API and places no actual calls. 244 245 Use `ORMA_DRY_RUN_FIXTURE` to select the simulated execution outcome: 246 - `completed` (default): Simulates an answered call with valid extraction. 247 - `failed`: Simulates an unanswered call or network failure. 248 - `no_result`: Simulates an answered call where result validation fails. 249 250 In dry-run mode, the dispatcher writes standard audit records to `call_events`: 251 - `dispatched`: Records synthetic dispatch with masked request details and `outbound_request_made: false`. 252 - `ingested`: Records extracted items and mentions from the chosen fixture. 253 - `finalised`: Records the final state and disposition with `billable: false`. 254 255 Setting `ORMA_DRY_RUN=false` enables live telephony. Real calls cost \$0.05 each after CALL-E's 20 initial free calls. 256 257 ## Credentials 258 259 Orma protects credentials strictly. The publishable key `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` is the only key included in the web client bundle. The build script `scripts/check-no-secret-key.mjs` runs during `npm run check` and fails the build if any secret key appears under `web/`. 260 261 The following secrets remain server-side only: 262 - `CALLE_API_KEY`: Authenticates outbound call requests to the CALL-E API. 263 - `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`: Grants administrative database privileges for functions, migrations, and seed scripts. 264 - `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD`: Authenticates direct database connections for migrations and local containers. 265 - `ORMA_VAULT_KEY`: Encrypts sensitive credentials in Supabase Vault. 266 - `ORMA_WEBHOOK_SECRET`: Authenticates inbound webhook requests from CALL-E. 267 - `ORMA_MATERIALISE_SECRET_KEY`: Authorises scheduled execution of the nightly materialise job. 268 - `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`: Authenticates bot calls to the Telegram Bot API. 269 - `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`: Validates inbound webhook requests from Telegram. 270 - `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS_JSON`: Authorises Vertex AI requests for speech transcription and pattern analysis. 271 - `RESEND_API_KEY`: Authenticates transactional email requests to Resend. 272 - `CF_DNS_API_TOKEN`: Authorises Cloudflare DNS and zone administration. 273 274 ## Consent and numbers 275 276 Orma accepts phone numbers in E.164 format only. The format requires a leading plus sign followed by 8 to 15 digits (`^\+[1-9]\d{7,14}$`). All documentation and examples use fictional numbers such as `+15555550100` or masked representations such as `+1 ••• ••• 0100`. 277 278 Orma records explicit user consent before placing any telephone call. Onboarding requires granting consent, stored as a durable audit row in the `consents` table: 279 280 ```sql 281 insert into public.consents (user_id, kind, text_version, source) 282 values ( 283 auth.uid(), 284 'outbound_calls', 285 'I authorize Orma to place automated daily telephone calls to my phone number and process audio for task extraction and pattern review.', 286 'web' 287 ) 288 ``` 289 290 The `tick` dispatcher checks for an active, unrevoked consent row before dialling. If a user revokes consent or if no consent row exists, the dispatcher skips the run without making a call. 291 292 ## Surfaces 293 294 Orma provides three distinct user and agent surfaces: 295 296 - **Web app (`orma.nryn.dev`)**: The primary interface for onboarding, scheduling, task review, call transcripts, and account settings. 297 - **Telegram bot (`@orma_tele_bot`)**: Handles quick task capture via text or voice notes, sends post-call receipts, and delivers weekly pattern summaries. 298 - **MCP server (`https://orma-api.nryn.dev/mcp`)**: Implements the Model Context Protocol over stateless Streamable HTTP. It exposes six tools (`add_item`, `list_items`, `retire_item`, `set_slot`, `get_last_call`, `get_patterns`) for external AI agents under user JWT authentication. Read [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) for endpoint details and setup instructions. 299 300 ### Third-party integrations 301 302 Orma relies on six third-party services: 303 - **CALL-E**: Places outbound phone calls, provides speech synthesis and recognition, and validates structured outputs. 304 - **Google Cloud Vertex AI (Gemini)**: Transcribes Telegram voice notes and drafts weekly pattern report prose from SQL facts. 305 - **Telegram Bot API**: Delivers bot notifications and ingests audio notes. 306 - **Resend**: Delivers magic link authentication emails and post-call receipts over an HTTP API. 307 - **Supabase**: Provides Postgres 17 with Row-Level Security, authentication, Vault secret storage, and Edge Functions. 308 - **Cloudflare**: Hosts the web frontend Worker and runs the API reverse proxy Worker. 309 310 ## Known limitations 311 312 1. **Missed calls are not retried**: Orma places each scheduled call once. If you decline or miss the call, Orma records disposition `not_answered`. The system does not attempt a redial or roll forward missed days. Open items remain on your list and appear in your next scheduled call. 313 314 2. **Unrecognised incoming numbers and spam flags**: Outbound calls originate from rotating telephone numbers provided by CALL-E. Because caller numbers rotate across calls, callees cannot save a static contact in advance. Handsets may display unrecognised numbers or automated spam warnings. Onboarding instructs users to expect an unfamiliar incoming number at their chosen slot. 315 316 ## Screens 317 318 The screenshots below show Orma running on a phone viewport with seeded demo data: 319 320 | Today | Items | 321 |---|---| 322 | ![Today screen](docs/screens/today.png) | ![Items screen](docs/screens/items.png) | 323 324 | Call History | Timeline | 325 |---|---| 326 | ![Call history screen](docs/screens/history.png) | ![Timeline screen](docs/screens/timeline.png) | 327 328 | Patterns | Settings | 329 |---|---| 330 | ![Patterns screen](docs/screens/patterns.png) | ![Settings screen](docs/screens/settings.png) | 331

No, the README isn't fine yet. It's well organised and its style is clean: no semicolons, no em dashes, no keys or real numbers. But I checked it against the code, and several instructions and claims are wrong. A reader following it would break a deploy, and the screenshots don't show the real app. T8.3 is still claimed and uncommitted, so it can be fixed before it lands.

**Wrong enough to break something or mislead**

| # | Section | Problem | What the code says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Deploy, step 4 and Credentials | `ORMA_VAULT_KEY` doesn't exist anywhere in the code. | The crons read `ORMA_MATERIALISE_SECRET_KEY` from **Vault**, created with `vault.create_secret`, holding a secret API key named `materialise`. |

## 3. The call

### It gives before it takes

Opening with "anything to add?" is extraction, and it gets ignored by day nine.
Opening with something you did not know — this is due tomorrow, you have said
this three times, this has sat for a month — earns the slot.

This is an ordering rule. The call **must** ask what is new, because capture is
half of what the product fixes. It just cannot lead with it. A cold "what's
new?" gets a blank, since nobody has their life paged in at 8am. Asked after
being walked through what is outstanding, the same question gets a better answer.

### Shape

1. **Land.** Say who you are and wait. Ask whether you can be heard and wait for a yes.
2. **Give.** One or two things you did not know. Overdue, repeated, aged.
3. **Walk.** What is open, briefly. Not the whole list.
4. **Take.** What needs capturing.
5. **Offer the exit.** Anything to let go of.
6. **Close.** Confirm tomorrow's slot. Hang up.

Target two minutes.

**Landing is a step, not a courtesy.** The first seconds of a phone call are
lost while the other person works out who is speaking, and phone audio is worse
than anyone designing for it assumes. So landing takes two beats.

> **Orma:** Hello. This is Orma.
> **You:** Hello.
> **Orma:** Can you hear me?
> **You:** Yes.

The first line is sacrificial. It carries nothing worth keeping and it is
expected to be missed. The second tests the channel, and the yes is the only
evidence that the line works. Nothing that matters is said before it arrives.

Give-before-take orders the check-in. It never licenses leading with content
nobody is ready to hear.

### Quitting is easy and unpunished

The failure mode is dodging, not forgetting. By week three you know what it is
going to ask and you decline the call rather than face it. That is churn from
working too well.

So someone can say *kill it, I am never doing this*, and Orma simply agrees. A
list you cannot retire from becomes a wall of shame, and a wall of shame is a
call you stop answering. Being allowed to drop something honestly is what keeps
the rest of the list truthful. It is also the demo beat nobody else will have.

---

Orma opens by landing the call, and your lines won't happen exactly as written: the call follows a set order and the model chooses its own wording. Everything below is from the task Orma actually sends to CALL-E (`supabase/functions/_shared/briefing.ts`, matching `docs/calle-call.md`) and the briefing SQL.

**How Orma introduces itself**

> **Orma:** Hello. This is Orma.
> *(waits for you to answer)*
> **Orma:** Can you hear me?
> *(waits for a yes)*

The task tells it to say those two lines exactly and to wait after each. If you don't clearly say yes, it repeats both once more, slowly. It also knows it's a machine and is told not to pretend otherwise.

**What the call actually does**

| Step | What Orma says |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | "Hello. This is Orma." then "Can you hear me?" |
| 3 | **"You've mentioned the dentist 3 times. It's been 34 days."** The briefing SQL builds this sentence from the database. Orma repeats it if you didn't hear it. |
| 4 | Walks the open items, naming each once, plus a one-line summary of the last call |
| 5 | Asks what's new and needs capturing |
| 6 | Offers the exit: "Anything on the list you want to drop?" |
| 7 | Confirms tomorrow's time and hangs up |

**How that differs from your script**

1. **The wording of the lead line.** It's "You've mentioned… 3 times. It's been 34 days", with contractions and the number as a digit. Spoken aloud, the 3 sounds like "three", so this part matches closely.
2. **When "Kill it" comes.** The natural moment is step 6, after the walk-through and the capture question. You can say "Kill it" straight after the lead line, but the task doesn't script a reply at that point, so Orma may carry on to step 4 first.
3. **"Done. It's gone." isn't scripted anywhere.** Step 6 says only "agree cleanly, don't argue". Orma might say "Okay, I've dropped it", or something close. The retirement itself is recorded after the call, from what you said (with the moment you said it), and then shows in Items, History and the Telegram receipt.
4. **Real calls drift.** On your 11 September test call, Orma read the lead line before landing the call, skipped the exit offer and left long silences. Plan for a few takes.

**If you want the video to match your script word for word**, the task needs a small change:
- step 3 lets you drop the item as soon as you hear it;
- the confirmation uses exactly "Done. It's gone.".

That change lives in the call engine, so it also means updating `briefing.ts`, `docs/calle-call.md` and the test that pins the task text word for word. Even then, the model's wording is likely but never guaranteed. Otherwise, write the demo video script around the real order: land, lead line, a short walk, the exit, "Kill it", Orma agrees.

content.text:
Yes, you can record the call now. You don't have to wait for P9 or P10, because the call doesn't go through the new UI. Production just needs to be set up first, and the audio has to be captured another way.

**Where production stands**
- **Empty:** no profiles, consents, slots, seeded items or scheduled calls, and no call has ever been placed.
- **Number check:** the live app is still the P6 version, where onboarding marks your number confirmed when you save it. P10 is built in the repo but not deployed: 2 migrations are unapplied and `confirm-phone` isn't deployed. That doesn't block the recording. Once P10 deploys, the database only clears confirmation if the number changes, so your account stays confirmed.

**Steps, in order**
1. **Sign up** at `orma.nryn.dev` with your own account and number. Agree to consent, and pick a call time about 10 minutes ahead.
2. **Seed your account.** Run `scripts/seed.ts --email <you> --i-confirmed-dry-run --apply` against production. It needs the service role key in the environment, and I need your go-ahead to run it. The call will then say "You've mentioned the dentist 3 times. It's been 34 days". It also walks the passport and groceries items, and says the last call captured one new item.
3. **Create the scheduled call.** `materialise` only runs nightly at 00:10 UTC, so trigger it once by hand, the same way I did this morning. Otherwise tonight is the earliest call.
4. **Turn dry run off:** `supabase secrets set ORMA_DRY_RUN=false`. You'll be the only profile, so only your phone can be called. Turn it back on straight after recording.
5. **Answer the call.** `tick` places it at that minute. Each take is one real call, which costs $0.05 once CALL-E's 20 free calls are used up.

**Recording the audio**
- **scrcpy probably can't do it.** Android generally blocks apps, scrcpy included, from recording phone-call audio. scrcpy will show the incoming call screen but will most likely record silence during the call.
- **CALL-E has no recording to download.** Its API returns no recording field, only the transcript with timestamps.
- **What works:** put the phone on speaker and record it with a second device, such as a laptop microphone or another phone. Use the CALL-E transcript for exact captions.

**If you need a second take**

content.text:
Here's the brief for your agent. It builds the same task Orma sends on a real call, places one call to your number and saves the transcript for captions, without touching Orma's database. Every name and shape below is from the repo.

**Brief for the agent: one-off demo call script**

**Where it lives:** outside the repository, for example `~/orma-demo/demo-call.ts`. AGENTS.md makes `calle.ts` the only code that may place a call, and the packaging script ships everything in `scripts/`, so this one-off must not live in the repo. Import from the repo using absolute paths.

**Imports**
- `renderCallTask` and the `Briefing` type from `/home/nryn/work/orma/supabase/functions/_shared/briefing.ts`
- `CALL_E_RESULT_SCHEMA` from `/home/nryn/work/orma/supabase/functions/_shared/calle.ts`

**Inputs**
- **Environment:** `CALLE_API_BASE` and `CALLE_API_KEY`, loaded from `/home/nryn/work/orma/.env` without printing them. Never `export` a secret in an interactive shell.
- **Flags:**
  - `--phone <E.164>`: your own number only, and it must match `^\+[1-9]\d{7,14}$`.
  - `--name <spoken name>`
  - `--take <n>`
  - `--confirm`: without it, the script prints the request and stops.

**The briefing,** written as literal values that match what the database would produce after seeding:
```ts
const briefing: Briefing = {
  user_name: name,
  open_count: 3,
  lead_line: "You've mentioned the dentist 3 times. It's been 34 days.",
  open_items: "- the dentist (id: demo-dentist)\n- renew the passport (id: demo-passport)\n- weekend groceries (id: demo-groceries)",
  last_call_summary: "Last call we wrote down 1 new item.",
  slot_local_time: "08:00",
};
const task = renderCallTask(briefing);
```

**The request**
- `POST ${CALLE_API_BASE}/v1/calls`
- **Headers:**
  - `authorization: Bearer ${CALLE_API_KEY}`
  - `content-type: application/json`
  - `idempotency-key: orma:demo:<YYYY-MM-DD>:take-<n>`, a new key for each take and the same key if the same take is retried.
- **Body:** `{ task, recipients: [{ phones: [phone] }], result_schema: CALL_E_RESULT_SCHEMA }`
- **Webhook:** leave out `webhook_url` and `metadata`, so no event reaches Orma. If CALL-E returns 422 saying `webhook_url` is required, stop and report. Don't point it at Orma's webhook.
- **Retries:** never retry automatically. On 409 or any error, print the status and stop.

**Behaviour**
1. **Without `--confirm`:** print the request with the phone number masked (for example `+91•••••••321`) and the full task text, then exit. Run this first and read the task.
2. **With `--confirm`:** place exactly one call and print the returned call id.
3. **Wait for the result:** wait 60 seconds, then `GET ${CALLE_API_BASE}/v1/calls/<id>` every 10 seconds until the status is terminal, giving up after 10 minutes.
4. **Save the result:** write the final JSON to `~/orma-demo/take-<n>.json`. It contains your real number and the transcript, so never commit or share it.
5. **Print captions:** turns come from `recipients[0].attempts[0].transcript_turns`, one line per turn, as `M:SS speaker: text`.

**Recording**
- **Audio:** put the phone on speaker and record it with a second device. Android usually blocks scrcpy from recording call audio.
- **Screen:** scrcpy is fine for the incoming-call screen.
- **Syncing:** start the recorder before running with `--confirm`, and use the transcript timings to line up captions.

**Cost and retakes:** each confirmed run is one real call, costing $0.05 once the 20 free calls are used up. Nothing in Orma changes, so a retake is just `--take <n+1> --confirm`, and the lead line stays "3 times, 34 days".

The call wording will be exactly what the live product sends, because it's the same template with the same kind of briefing.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Package Orma into a checkout of CALLE-AI/awesome-phone-call-agents.
#
# Usage: scripts/package-list-pr.sh <list-repo-checkout>
#
# The copy comes from the committed HEAD, never the working tree. It lands in
# apps/web/orma/ and leaves out proxy/, dev-diary/, design/ and agent files.
# The script then scans the copy, runs the tests inside it, adds the index row,
# and runs the list repository's own validator. Any failure stops the run.

set -euo pipefail

target="${1:-}"
if [ -z "$target" ] || [ ! -f "$target/scripts/validate_repository.py" ] || [ ! -d "$target/apps" ]; then
  echo "usage: scripts/package-list-pr.sh <checkout of awesome-phone-call-agents>" >&2
  exit 2
fi

src="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
target="$(cd "$target" && pwd)"
dest="$target/apps/web/orma"

fail() {
  echo "package-list-pr: $*" >&2
  exit 1
}

echo "package-list-pr: copying HEAD $(git -C "$src" rev-parse --short HEAD) into apps/web/orma"
rm -rf "$dest"
mkdir -p "$dest"
git -C "$src" archive --format=tar HEAD \
  web supabase scripts testdata docs .env.example README.md \
  | tar -x -C "$dest"
rm -f "$dest/scripts/package-list-pr.sh"

# The copy has no proxy Worker, so its README says what stands in for it.
python3 - "$dest/README.md" <<'PY'
import sys
path = sys.argv[1]
text = open(path, encoding="utf-8").read()
note = """## About this copy

This directory packages Orma for the CALL-E awesome list. It includes the web app, the Supabase schema and functions, the local stack script and the recorded fixtures.

It leaves out the `proxy/` Worker. That Worker is a plain pass-through to the Supabase project. The web app and the functions refuse any API URL containing `supabase.co`, so a self-hosted deployment needs its own reverse proxy in front of the project. Point `ORMA_API_URL` at that proxy.

The local walkthrough below needs no proxy and places no calls.

"""
marker = "## What Orma is"
if marker not in text:
    sys.exit("README has no 'What Orma is' section to anchor the note")
open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(text.replace(marker, note + marker, 1))
PY

echo "package-list-pr: scanning the copy"
secret_patterns='sb_secret_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}|eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}|re_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}|[0-9]{8,10}:AA[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----|"private_key"[[:space:]]*:'
if hits="$(grep -rlIE "$secret_patterns" "$dest" 2>/dev/null)"; then
  fail "key-shaped text in: ${hits//$dest\//}"
fi

found_env="$(find "$dest" -name '.env' -o -name '.env.*' ! -name '.env.example' | head -1)"
[ -z "$found_env" ] || fail "an env file was copied: ${found_env#$dest/}"

big="$(find "$dest" -type f -size +5M | head -1)"
[ -z "$big" ] || fail "file over 5 MB: ${big#$dest/}"

if [ -f "$src/.env" ]; then
  owner_digits="$(grep -E '^ORMA_OWNER_PHONE=' "$src/.env" | head -1 | cut -d= -f2- | tr -cd '0-9')"
  if [ "${#owner_digits}" -ge 10 ]; then
    if hits="$(grep -rlIF "${owner_digits: -10}" "$dest" 2>/dev/null)"; then
      fail "the operator's phone number appears in: ${hits//$dest\//}"
    fi
  fi
fi

operator_email="$(git -C "$src" config user.email || true)"
if [ -n "$operator_email" ] && hits="$(grep -rlIiF "$operator_email" "$dest" 2>/dev/null)"; then
  fail "the operator's email appears in: ${hits//$dest\//}"
fi

if hits="$(grep -rlIF 'pyuubklpkhjngiqqwypf.supabase.co' "$dest" 2>/dev/null)"; then
  fail "the project host appears in: ${hits//$dest\//}"
fi

echo "package-list-pr: running Deno tests in the copy"
(
  cd "$dest"
  for suite in dispatch-mode finalise ingest poll calle receipt deliver-telegram; do
    files="supabase/functions/_shared/$suite.ts"
    [ -f "supabase/functions/_shared/${suite}_tests.ts" ] && files="$files supabase/functions/_shared/${suite}_tests.ts"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    timeout 600 deno test --quiet --allow-read --allow-env --allow-net=127.0.0.1 $files >/dev/null \
      || fail "deno tests failed for $suite"
  done
  timeout 600 deno test --quiet --allow-read --allow-env supabase/functions/tick/index.ts >/dev/null \
    || fail "deno tests failed for tick"
)

echo "package-list-pr: running npm run check in the copy"
(
  cd "$dest/web"
  timeout 900 npm ci --no-audit --no-fund --loglevel=error >/dev/null || fail "npm ci failed"
  PUBLIC_ORMA_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:54321 REDACTED \
    timeout 900 npm run --silent check >/dev/null || fail "npm run check failed"
)
rm -rf "$dest/web/node_modules" "$dest/web/.svelte-kit"

index="$target/apps/README.md"
if ! grep -qF '[`web/orma`](web/orma/)' "$index"; then
  python3 - "$index" <<'PY'
import sys
path = sys.argv[1]
row = ("| [`web/orma`](web/orma/) | TypeScript / SvelteKit / Deno / Supabase | "
       "Daily two-minute accountability calls. SQL briefs CALL-E, so the call leads with what you keep "
       "not doing, captures new items, and lets you drop one without argument. Consent rows, a one-time "
       "code call before any number is dialled daily, cancel and pause, plus Telegram and MCP surfaces. "
       "Dry run by default, with a local Supabase stack and recorded fixtures. |")
lines = open(path, encoding="utf-8").read().split("\n")
for i, line in enumerate(lines):
    if line.strip() == "| --- | --- | --- |":
        lines.insert(i + 1, row)
        break
else:
    sys.exit("apps/README.md has no app table")
open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write("\n".join(lines))
PY
fi

echo "package-list-pr: running the list repository's validator"
(cd "$target" && timeout 600 python3 scripts/validate_repository.py >/dev/null) || fail "validate_repository.py failed"

files="$(find "$dest" -type f | wc -l)"
size="$(du -sh "$dest" | cut -f1)"
echo "package-list-pr: done. $files files, $size, in apps/web/orma"

## Summary

Orma is a daily two-minute accountability call. It rings at a time you chose, leads with what you keep not doing, asks what needs capturing, and lets you drop an item without argument.

The call arrives already knowing. SQL counts mentions and ages, and those numbers are rendered into the CALL-E task before dispatch, so the model phrases facts it never computed: "You've mentioned the dentist 3 times. It's been 34 days." A structured result schema writes captured items, retirements with transcript evidence offsets, and commitments back to Postgres.

Orma owns the scheduler, following this repository's provider-separation principle. `pg_cron` materialises runs, a minute tick claims them with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and dispatches with a stable idempotency key, and results come back through a re-fetched webhook and polling.

Surfaces: a SvelteKit web app for setup and review, a Telegram bot for text and voice capture and receipts, and an MCP server with six tools under the user's own JWT and row-level security.

The app lives in `apps/web/orma/` with its own README. It also adds one row to `apps/README.md`.

## Type

- [ ] New skill
- [x] New runnable app
- [ ] New workflow plugin
- [ ] New provider adapter
- [ ] New scheduler recipe
- [ ] README awesome-list entry
- [ ] Safety or documentation update
- [ ] Validation or tooling update

## Checklist

- [x] Repository-facing content is written in English.
- [x] Branch name, commit messages, and PR title follow `docs/git-naming-conventions.md`.
- [x] No secrets, tokens, private phone numbers, call recordings, or private transcripts are included. The recorded CALL-E fixtures keep the provider's response shapes, and their conversation turns are synthetic, as `testdata/calle/README.md` states.
- [x] Real-world side effects are clearly described. The README has a side-effects table covering calls, the three cron jobs, the confirmation call, Telegram messages, pattern report email, and stored voice notes.
- [x] Phone numbers are masked in documentation and test fixtures unless they are clearly fictional.
- [x] Recurring workflows include cancellation behavior. Users can cancel today's call, pause all calls, revoke consent, or delete the account. Operators can unschedule each cron job and turn dry run back on.
- [x] Runnable code has a dry-run, fake-server, or no-call path by default. `ORMA_DRY_RUN` defaults to true and fails closed when unset.
- [x] `python3 scripts/validate_repository.py` passes.

## Safety

- **Explicit intent.** No call is placed without a consent row that stores the exact wording shown, a slot the user chose, and a confirmed number.
- **Authorized destinations.** Anyone can sign up, so a typed number is not trusted. A one-time call reads a six-digit code, and the user enters it in the app. Only then does the server set the confirmed flag. Users cannot set it themselves, and changing the number clears it. Attempts are rate limited and never redialled.
- **No duplicate calls.** Claims use `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and every dispatch carries a unique idempotency key. A 409 is recorded as a failure, never retried.
- **No redial after an ambiguous outcome.** Unanswered and failed calls are recorded and never retried.
- **Credentials.** Only the publishable key reaches the browser, and the build fails if a secret key appears under `web/`. Every function reaches Supabase through a configured front door, never a project host.

## Verification

Run locally with no hosted services and no calls:

- `scripts/p6-local-stack.sh up`, then the web app against it, as the README walkthrough describes.
- Deno suites for dispatch, dry run, ingest, polling, finalisation, receipts, Telegram delivery and the tick all pass inside the packaged copy.
- `npm run check` passes inside the packaged copy.
- `python3 scripts/validate_repository.py` passes on this branch.

## Disclosure

The demo video records a real call to the author's own phone. The history that call reads is seeded by `scripts/seed.ts`, and every seeded row is marked `seeded = true` or carries an `orma:seed:` idempotency key.
